explanation: No coherent pattern: strong activations fall on a mix of tokens such as place-name pieces in addresses ('Overland Park', 'Urbana'), digits, code identifiers, and ordinary function words, with no shared token or context.

Fires on the function word right after a role/usage verb or attorney listing: the article or preposition after 'used as', 'served as', 'employed as', 'as the', and especially 'for' in court attorney credits ('Smith, City, for appellant'). Weak on other function words.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces in words split into several tokens, especially 'ipop'/'op' in apolipoprotein/lipoprotein/vasopressin, plus scattered other word-internal fragments and abbreviation pieces (EPATH, LSA-R, 'best'seller). Strength depends on the token being a piece of a longer word.

Fires on connecting tokens inside date, place and event phrases: 'of' in 'first Wednesday of', 'Isle of', 'Archdiocese of', 'head of'; the comma after a weekday or town name at a sentence start ('On Thursday,', 'In the town of Celina,'); 'at' after a match time. Mostly news/locational framing.

Fires on an adjective (often ending -al/-ical/-ic) that begins a technical or institutional compound noun phrase: 'operational amplifier', 'cosmic microwave', 'planetary protection', 'numerical transfer', 'judicial release', 'Medical marijuana', 'industrial railway'. Weaker on suffix pieces of such adjectives.
Heterogeneous: '.Collections' in 'using System.Collections', code operator pieces, and assorted mid-sentence words and names ('Orient', 'asthma', 'Aleppo', 'along'). No common token or context.

Fires on a slash, or on the token right after a slash or dot, inside paths, URLs, include/require paths and slash-joined pairs ('clang/', 'conversations/new', 'MUM1/IRF4', dates like 18/07, 'wikimedia.org'). The token next to the separator matters most.
Mixture: 'nil' in Go/Obj-C 'err != nil' and similar null checks, '\le' in LaTeX 'leq', the '-ly' suffix in 'Firstly'/'initially', and other word-internal subword pieces of rare words and names.

Fires on the first token of a new sentence or clause in Q&A or programming prose, often right after a code block or a preceding sentence ('In this query,', 'Note that', 'I', 'Here is', 'These figures'), i.e. where the writer resumes explaining. Weaker on later tokens.

Fires on control-flow continuation tokens in code: 'else' after a closing brace, '#else' in preprocessor blocks, 'default:' in switch statements, and the indentation whitespace just before a closing brace or else. Weak on prose words like 'despite' or 'since'.

No clear single theme. Strong activations come on varied tokens in mid-sentence, often after 'and', 'or' or a parenthesis ('and other empires', 'but not', '(and many downs)', '(well'), plus unrelated names and code tokens.

Fires on the verb in the idioms 'take place' and 'take effect' ('took', 'taken', 'take') and on 'into' in 'came into effect' / 'take into account/consideration'. Weaker on other light-verb or fixed-phrase tokens.

Fires in biomedical and materials-science abstracts on tokens inside noun phrases about effects or applications ('onset of', 'normal neurological function', 'inhibits growth', 'bone tissue', 'for diabetics'). Activation depends on scientific-abstract context more than on the token itself.

Fires on the completing subword or second word of technical compound terms: 'sh-iny' (R Shiny), 'liquid crystal display', 'reverse phase', 'light-emitting diodes', 'ultrasonography', 'Longitudinal'. There are also unrelated hits on 'I' and 'can' in conversational text.
Mixture: adverbs and modifiers ('really', 'always', 'recently', 'equally', 'respectfully'), Japanese text tokens, and path pieces like '/apimachinery'. No shared token or context.

Fires on word-internal subword pieces of technical, chemical or medical terms ('Rietv-eld', 'Thal-assa-emia', 'polyn-ucle-otide', '-ethyl', '-rophy', '-omers') and identifier pieces in code. Strength depends on the token being a continuation inside a jargon word.

Mixture: the space before the year in dates ('29 October 2016', 'Mon, 02 Mar 2015'), the colon after 'Greek' in Wikipedia etymologies, 'null' in null checks, and 'of' in the MIT license phrase 'free of charge'.

Fires on assorted tokens with no shared meaning: the preposition 'in' after a verb phrase ('explain their album in', 'expressed in'), name or word pieces ('Molot', 'Phantoms'), Japanese particles, and version digits.

Fires most strongly on 'links' in the Wikipedia section heading 'References / External links'. It also fires on unrelated boilerplate and other tokens ('close this message', 'Content-type', 'nearest 10', 'receive a copy').

Fires on 'agile'/'Agile' (and '-ile' in 'ag-ile') in software and business methodology contexts. It fires weakly on related jargon (DevSecOps, agility, continuous integration) and on scattered other tokens.

Fires on uncommon, fairly specific content words, often the first piece of a rarer word: occupations ('chiropractor', 'guitarist', 'gymnast'), evaluative adjectives ('gruesome', 'catchy', 'dysfunctional', 'polite') and other topical nouns. There is no single semantic field.
